questions.q: What are the two discussion prompts given in the "Talking about the Text" section of the NCERT textbook for "Tomorrow"?
questions.a: The two prompts are: (1) 'Every mental state, even madness, has its equilibrium based upon self-esteem. Its disturbance causes unhappiness.' (2) Joyce's 'Eveline' and Conrad's 'Tomorrow' are thematically similar. A wrong answer (e.g., listing comprehension questions or appreciation questions) reveals the student cannot distinguish between discussion prompts for oral debate and written analysis tasks — a critical error for internal assessment preparation.

questions.q: A student says: "Captain Hagberd is crazy because he waits for his son every day." Why is this an insufficient discussion contribution for Class 12 level?
questions.a: It states a plot fact without interpretive depth, textual evidence, or engagement with the prompt's conceptual framework (self-esteem equilibrium). A Class 12 discussion requires analyzing *how* the madness functions — e.g., "Hagberd's 'tomorrow' ritual maintains his self-esteem by deferring confrontation with reality, as shown when he reacts with 'horror and incredulity' to Bessie's doubt (p.46)." A wrong answer reveals confusion between plot summary and literary analysis.

questions.q: During a discussion on Prompt 1, a peer argues: "Hagberd's madness is harmless — he just digs his garden." Using the "Evidence → Interpretation → Implication" structure, formulate a 3-sentence counter-argument that references the stranger/Harry scene.
questions.a: Evidence: When Harry arrives, Hagberd throws a shovel at him and bolts the door (p.53), shouting "Don't you have anything to do with him. It will spoil everything." Interpretation: The madness is not harmless but actively defensive — it repels the very return it awaits. Implication: The "equilibrium" depends on the *idea* of return, not the reality; the son's presence shatters the self-esteem structure. A weak answer would omit the textual moment or fail to link to the prompt's "self-esteem" concept.

questions.q: Compare the narrative technique of "story within a story" (mentioned in the author bio) with the way Hagberd's past is revealed through the barber's gossip and Hagberd's own monologues to Bessie. What is the effect of this layered revelation?
questions.a: The barber's gossip (pp.40-42) gives an external, mocking perspective; Hagberd's monologues to Bessie (pp.43-45) give an internal, rationalized perspective; the narrator's description (p.43) bridges both. The effect: we see madness constructed socially (barber's "treatment") and maintained intimately (Bessie's complicity), making the final collapse more tragic. A partial answer would only list sources without analyzing the *perspectival tension* they create.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Bessie is as complicit in Hagberd's madness as he is." Defend or refute using at least two textual instances where she actively sustains or challenges his delusion.
questions.a: Refute with nuance: She sustains it by never contradicting him ("What for should I? It would only have made him miserable" — p.56) and half-believing it herself ("It was easier to half believe it myself"). But she challenges it once, asking "your son may not even want to look at me" (p.51), triggering his "horror and incredulity" — proving she knows the fragility. A one-sided answer (only complicit or only resistant) misses the psychological complexity Conrad builds.

questions.q: Create a 2-minute opening statement for a debate on Prompt 2 ("Joyce's 'Eveline' and Conrad's 'Tomorrow' are thematically similar") that identifies one shared theme, one structural parallel, and one key difference — without retelling either plot.
questions.a: Shared theme: Paralysis of the will — Eveline cannot board the ship; Hagberd cannot accept the present. Structural parallel: Both use a threshold moment (window/door) where the past/future collide. Key difference: Eveline's paralysis is internal (fear, duty); Hagberd's is performative (ritualized waiting sustained by another). A poor answer would summarize plots or list vague similarities ("both about family") without analytical precision.
